tool.name: Google Cloud
tool.tagline: Google's public cloud for compute, data, networking and AI
tool.description: Google Cloud is Google's public cloud platform: virtual machines, serverless containers, Kubernetes, managed databases, BigQuery analytics and Vertex AI, all on Google's global network and managed through one resource hierarchy and IAM model. Learning it lets you deploy, secure and run production systems on infrastructure used by many of the world's largest workloads.

concepts.name: Regions, zones and the service map
concepts.summary: How Google Cloud is laid out physically (regions, zones) and how its services group into compute, storage, data and AI.
concepts.why: Every resource you create lives in a location, and that choice drives latency, availability, price and compliance.
concepts.body:
Google Cloud is a catalog of managed services running in Google's data centers. Before creating anything you need two ideas: **location** and **resource scope**.

A **region** is a geographic area such as `us-central1` or `europe-west1`. Each region contains three or more **zones** (`europe-west1-b`), which are isolated failure domains: separate power, cooling and networking. Some services also offer **multi-regions** (`US`, `EU`) that replicate data across regions.

Resources have a scope that follows from this:

- **Zonal**: a VM and its persistent disk live in one zone. If that zone fails, they are unavailable.
- **Regional**: subnets, regional managed instance groups, Cloud Run services and Cloud SQL HA instances span the zones of a region.
- **Global**: VPC networks, firewall rules, images and the global external load balancer.

The services fall into rough families: compute (Compute Engine, GKE, Cloud Run, Cloud Run functions), storage and databases (Cloud Storage, Cloud SQL, Firestore, Spanner, BigQuery), networking (VPC, Load Balancing, Cloud CDN, Cloud NAT), operations (Logging, Monitoring) and AI (Vertex AI).

Pick a region close to your users, check that the services you need are available there, and keep related resources in the same region: traffic between regions is slower and is billed as egress.
concepts.code:
# List regions and the zones of one region
gcloud compute regions list --format="value(name)" | head -5
# africa-south1
# asia-east1
# asia-east2
# ...
gcloud compute zones list --filter="region:europe-west1" --format="value(name)"
# europe-west1-b
# europe-west1-c
# europe-west1-d
takeaways: A region holds 3+ isolated zones
Resources are zonal, regional or global
Keep chatty resources in one region to avoid latency and egress charges
pitfalls: Running a single VM in one zone and calling it highly available.

quiz.q: Which resource is zonal in Google Cloud?
quiz.explain: A VM and its disks live in one zone; VPC networks, firewall rules and global load balancers are global.

concepts.name: The console and Cloud Shell
concepts.summary: Find your way around the Google Cloud console and use Cloud Shell, a free browser terminal with gcloud already signed in.
concepts.why: It is the fastest way to start: no local install, the right credentials and the tools preinstalled.
concepts.body:
The **Google Cloud console** (console.cloud.google.com) is the web UI. The project picker at the top decides which project you are looking at; most confusion for beginners comes from being in the wrong project. The navigation menu lists every product, and you can pin the ones you use. The search bar finds products, resources and docs.

Click the terminal icon to open **Cloud Shell**: a small Linux VM in your browser with `gcloud`, `kubectl`, `terraform`, `docker`, Python, Node.js and Git preinstalled, already authenticated as you. Key facts:

- Your `$HOME` is a 5 GB persistent disk; everything outside it resets between sessions.
- The selected project is exported as `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT`.
- **Cloud Shell Editor** gives you a VS Code-style editor on the same machine.
- Sessions end after inactivity, and the home disk is deleted if you do not use Cloud Shell for 120 days.

Use the console to explore and learn what exists, and Cloud Shell or the CLI to do things repeatably. Most console pages have an "Equivalent command" or "Equivalent code" option that shows the gcloud command or REST request, which is a good way to learn the CLI.
concepts.code:
# Inside Cloud Shell
echo $GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT        # shop-dev-4821
gcloud config list
# [core]
# account = you@example.com
# project = shop-dev-4821

gcloud projects list --format="table(projectId,name)"
df -h $HOME | tail -1             # ~5G persistent home disk
takeaways: Always check the project picker before changing anything
Cloud Shell comes authenticated with the common CLIs installed
Only $HOME persists in Cloud Shell
pitfalls: Installing tools system-wide in Cloud Shell and expecting them to survive the next session.

quiz.q: You installed a tool with apt in Cloud Shell yesterday and it is gone today. Why?
options: Only the home directory persists between sessions
Cloud Shell deletes tools after 24 hours
apt is blocked in Cloud Shell
quiz.explain: Cloud Shell's VM is recreated each session; only the 5 GB home disk is persistent.

concepts.name: Organization, folders and projects
concepts.summary: The resource hierarchy: an organization node, nested folders and projects that own every resource, and what is inherited down the tree.
concepts.why: Projects are the unit of billing, quotas and API enablement, and policies set higher up flow down to them.
concepts.body:
Every Google Cloud resource belongs to exactly one **project**. Projects can sit under **folders**, and folders under an **organization** node that is tied to your company's Google Workspace or Cloud Identity domain.

A project has three identifiers:

- **Project ID**: globally unique, chosen by you, immutable (`shop-prod-4821`). Used in commands and APIs.
- **Project number**: assigned by Google, also immutable; appears in service agent emails.
- **Name**: a display label you can change.

The project is the boundary for enabled APIs, quotas, billing linkage and most IAM grants. A common layout is one project per application per environment (`shop-dev`, `shop-prod`), grouped in folders such as `Production` and `Non-production`, or by team.

Two things flow down the tree: **IAM allow policies** (a role granted on a folder applies to every project inside) and **organization policies** (guardrails such as allowed regions). A child can add permissions but cannot remove what a parent granted.

Accounts without an organization (a personal Gmail) can still create projects; they just have no folders or org-wide policies. Deleting a project shuts it down and schedules permanent deletion after a 30-day recovery window.
concepts.code:
# Create a project inside a folder and make it the default
gcloud projects create shop-dev-4821 --name="Shop dev" --folder=123456789012
gcloud config set project shop-dev-4821

gcloud projects describe shop-dev-4821 --format="value(projectNumber,parent.type,parent.id)"
# 987654321098  folder  123456789012

# Walk up the tree
gcloud projects get-ancestors shop-dev-4821
# ID              TYPE
# shop-dev-4821   project
# 123456789012    folder
# 555555555555    organization
takeaways: Every resource lives in one project
Project ID is unique and permanent; the name is just a label
IAM and org policies set on a folder or the org are inherited
pitfalls: Putting dev and prod in one project, so one IAM grant or quota affects both.

quiz.q: A user has Viewer on a folder. What can they see in a project inside that folder?
options: Nothing until granted on the project
Everything Viewer allows, inherited from the folder
quiz.explain: Allow policies are inherited down the hierarchy, so the folder grant applies to every project inside.

concepts.name: The gcloud CLI
concepts.summary: Install and initialise gcloud, manage named configurations, enable APIs, and shape output with --format and --filter.
concepts.why: gcloud is how you script, automate and reproduce everything you click in the console.
concepts.body:
The **gcloud CLI** (part of the Google Cloud SDK, alongside `bq` and the legacy `gsutil`) drives almost every service. Commands follow `gcloud GROUP [SUBGROUP] ACTION`, e.g. `gcloud compute instances list`.

Getting set up:

- `gcloud init` signs you in and picks a default project and region.
- `gcloud auth login` authenticates the CLI itself as your user.
- `gcloud config set project ID` and `gcloud config set compute/region europe-west1` set defaults, so you can omit `--project` and `--region`.

**Configurations** are named sets of these properties. Create one per context (`dev`, `prod`, a client) and switch with `gcloud config configurations activate prod`. Pass `--configuration` or `--project` for one-off commands.

A service must be **enabled** in a project before its API can be used: `gcloud services enable run.googleapis.com`. A "SERVICE_DISABLED" or "API has not been used in project" error means exactly this.

For scripting, every list or describe command accepts `--format` (`json`, `yaml`, `value(field)`, `table(...)`) and `--filter` (server- or client-side filtering on fields). `value()` gives bare values, perfect for shell variables.

Prefix `beta` or `alpha` to reach preview features, and add `--help` to any command for its full reference.
concepts.code:
gcloud config configurations create dev
gcloud config set project shop-dev-4821
gcloud config set compute/region europe-west1
gcloud config configurations list          # IS_ACTIVE marks the current one

gcloud services enable run.googleapis.com artifactregistry.googleapis.com
gcloud services list --enabled --filter="name:run" --format="value(name)"
# run.googleapis.com

# Capture a value for scripting
PROJECT_NUMBER=$(gcloud projects describe shop-dev-4821 --format="value(projectNumber)")
echo $PROJECT_NUMBER                        # 987654321098
takeaways: Use named configurations to switch between projects safely
Enable an API before using its service
--format=value(...) and --filter make gcloud scriptable
pitfalls: Running a destructive command against the wrong project because the active configuration was not the one you assumed.

quiz.q: A command fails with 'API has not been used in project ... or it is disabled'. What is the fix?
options: Enable the service with gcloud services enable
Switch to the beta command group
quiz.explain: Each service's API must be enabled per project before it can be called.

concepts.name: Billing accounts and the free tier
concepts.summary: How projects are linked to billing accounts, what the free trial and Always Free tier cover, and what happens when billing is removed.
concepts.why: Nothing paid runs without a billing account, and understanding the link prevents surprise bills and surprise outages.
concepts.body:
A **Cloud Billing account** holds the payment method and receives the charges. Each project is linked to at most one billing account; one billing account usually pays for many projects. Paid services refuse to work in a project with no billing linked.

Roles are separate from project roles: **Billing Account Administrator** manages the account, **Billing Account User** may link projects to it, and **Billing Account Viewer** reads costs. To link a project you need Billing Account User on the account and the right to change billing on the project (for example Project Owner or Project Billing Manager).

New customers get a **free trial** credit (USD 300 for 90 days at the time of writing). Separately, the **Free Tier** gives small monthly allowances that never expire, such as one e2-micro VM in certain US regions and a few GB of Cloud Storage in US regions, plus free quotas in services like Cloud Run, Pub/Sub and BigQuery.

If you **unlink billing** (or a budget automation does it), paid resources are stopped and may be deleted. That is a blunt kill switch, not a cost control. For day-to-day control you set **budgets** and alerts, covered later.

Costs appear in the console's Billing reports within hours; for detailed analysis export them to BigQuery.
concepts.code:
gcloud billing accounts list
# ACCOUNT_ID            NAME              OPEN
# 01AB23-45CD67-89EF01  Main billing      True

gcloud billing projects link shop-dev-4821 --billing-account=01AB23-45CD67-89EF01
gcloud billing projects describe shop-dev-4821 --format="value(billingEnabled)"
# True
takeaways: One billing account pays for many projects; a project has at most one
Billing roles are granted on the billing account, not the project
Unlinking billing stops paid resources, so it is not a gentle cost control
pitfalls: Assuming a budget caps spending; budgets only alert unless you automate an action.

quiz.q: What do you need to link a project to a billing account?
options: Billing Account User on the account plus billing rights on the project
quiz.explain: Linking needs permission on both sides: use the billing account, and change billing on the project.

concepts.name: IAM: principals, roles and allow policies
concepts.summary: Who can do what: principals, basic vs predefined roles, allow-policy bindings and how inheritance combines them.
concepts.why: IAM decides every API call in Google Cloud; most access problems and many security incidents trace back to it.
concepts.body:
**Identity and Access Management (IAM)** answers "who can do what on which resource". An **allow policy** attached to a resource (org, folder, project, or an individual bucket, topic, secret...) contains **bindings**: a role plus a list of principals.

**Principals** include `user:ada@example.com`, `group:devs@example.com`, `serviceAccount:app@proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com`, `domain:example.com`, and special ones like `allUsers` (anyone on the internet).

A **role** is a named set of **permissions** such as `storage.objects.get`. Three kinds:

- **Basic** roles: Owner, Editor, Viewer. Broad and coarse; avoid in production.
- **Predefined** roles: curated per service, e.g. `roles/storage.objectViewer`, `roles/run.developer`. Use these by default.
- **Custom** roles: your own permission list when no predefined role fits.

The effective policy on a resource is the **union** of its own policy and every ancestor's. Grants only add access; to take something away you remove the binding where it was made (or use deny policies, an advanced feature).

Good practice: grant roles to **groups**, not individuals; grant at the lowest level that works; prefer predefined roles over Editor. `gcloud projects get-iam-policy` shows bindings, and the console's Policy Troubleshooter explains why a principal has or lacks a permission.
concepts.code:
# Let a group read objects in one bucket only
gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding gs://shop-dev-assets \
  --member="group:frontend@example.com" --role="roles/storage.objectViewer"

# Project-wide grant to a user
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding shop-dev-4821 \
  --member="user:ada@example.com" --role="roles/run.developer"

# Who has which role on the project?
gcloud projects get-iam-policy shop-dev-4821 \
  --flatten="bindings[].members" --format="table(bindings.role,bindings.members)"

# Which permissions are in a role?
gcloud iam roles describe roles/storage.objectViewer --format="value(includedPermissions)"
takeaways: A binding = role + principals, attached to a resource
Prefer predefined roles over Owner/Editor/Viewer
Effective access is the union of the resource's and all ancestors' policies
Grant to groups at the lowest level that works
pitfalls: Granting Editor to make an error go away; it gives write access to nearly every service in the project.

quiz.q: Alice has roles/storage.admin on the project and no binding on bucket B. Can she delete objects in B?
options: Yes, the project grant is inherited by the bucket
No, bucket-level policies override project ones
Only if the bucket is public
quiz.explain: Allow policies are additive and inherited, so a project-level role applies to every bucket in it.

quiz.q: Which principal makes a resource readable by anyone on the internet?
quiz.explain: allUsers means any caller, authenticated or not.

concepts.name: Service accounts
concepts.summary: Identities for workloads: create service accounts, attach them to resources, and avoid long-lived keys.
concepts.why: Every VM, Cloud Run service and pipeline calls Google APIs as some service account; least privilege starts here.
concepts.body:
A **service account** is an identity for software, not a person. Its email looks like `app-sa@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com`. Like users, it receives IAM roles; unlike users, it has no password.

The safe way to use one is to **attach** it to a resource: a VM, a Cloud Run service, a function, a GKE workload, a Cloud Build trigger. Code running there gets short-lived tokens automatically from the metadata server; no secret ever touches disk.

Two separate permission questions:

- What can the service account do? Grant roles **to** it (e.g. `roles/pubsub.publisher` on a topic).
- Who may use it? To attach a service account to a resource you need `roles/iam.serviceAccountUser` **on** that service account. This stops someone who can deploy from borrowing a powerful identity.

Google also creates **default service accounts** (e.g. the Compute Engine default `PROJECT_NUMBER-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com`), and **service agents** that Google services use internally. Prefer a dedicated, minimal service account per workload over the defaults.

**Service account keys** (JSON files) are long-lived credentials that leak easily. Avoid them: use attached accounts inside Google Cloud, impersonation for humans, and Workload Identity Federation for workloads outside. Many organizations block key creation with an org policy.
concepts.code:
PROJECT=shop-dev-4821
gcloud iam service-accounts create orders-api --display-name="Orders API"
SA=orders-api@$PROJECT.iam.gserviceaccount.com

# What the workload may do: publish to one topic
gcloud pubsub topics add-iam-policy-binding orders \
  --member="serviceAccount:$SA" --role="roles/pubsub.publisher"

# Who may deploy things that run as it
gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding $SA \
  --member="group:orders-devs@example.com" --role="roles/iam.serviceAccountUser"

# Attach it to a Cloud Run service
gcloud run deploy orders-api --image=us-docker.pkg.dev/cloudrun/container/hello \
  --region=europe-west1 --service-account=$SA
takeaways: Attach service accounts to resources instead of using key files
One minimal service account per workload
serviceAccountUser on the SA controls who can run code as it
pitfalls: Downloading a JSON key to test locally and committing it to Git.
Leaving workloads on the default compute service account with broad roles.

quiz.q: Bob can deploy Cloud Run services but gets a permission error when setting --service-account=admin-sa. What is missing?
quiz.explain: Attaching a service account requires actAs permission (serviceAccountUser) on that specific account.

concepts.name: Compute Engine VMs
concepts.summary: Create, connect to and manage virtual machines: machine types, images, disks, SSH and Spot VMs.
concepts.why: VMs are the most flexible compute option and the base layer under GKE and many managed services.
concepts.body:
**Compute Engine** runs virtual machines in a zone. When creating one you choose:

- **Machine type**: family plus size, e.g. `e2-medium` (cost-optimised, shared-core options), `n4-standard-4` (general purpose), `c4-` (compute-optimised), `t2d-`/`t2a-` (scale-out, Arm in t2a). Custom shapes are possible on some families.
- **Boot image**: public images from projects like `debian-cloud` or `ubuntu-os-cloud`, chosen by **image family** to get the latest version.
- **Disks**: a boot disk plus optional Persistent Disk or Hyperdisk volumes; they outlive the VM unless set to auto-delete.
- **Service account and scopes**, network and subnet, and whether it gets an external IP.

Connect with `gcloud compute ssh`, which creates and propagates SSH keys for you (or uses OS Login when enabled). With `--tunnel-through-iap` you can reach VMs that have no external IP.

**Startup scripts** (metadata key `startup-script`) run at every boot; good for simple setup. A stopped VM stops compute billing, but its disks and reserved static IPs are still charged.

**Spot VMs** (`--provisioning-model=SPOT`) cost much less but can be preempted at any time with 30 seconds' notice: great for batch jobs and fault-tolerant workers, never for a single stateful server.
concepts.code:
gcloud compute instances create web-1 \
  --zone=europe-west1-b --machine-type=e2-medium \
  --image-family=debian-12 --image-project=debian-cloud \
  --tags=http-server --metadata=startup-script='#!/bin/bash
apt-get update && apt-get install -y nginx'

gcloud compute instances list --format="table(name,zone.basename(),status,networkInterfaces[0].accessConfigs[0].natIP)"
# NAME   ZONE            STATUS   NAT_IP
# web-1  europe-west1-b  RUNNING  34.76.12.34

gcloud compute ssh web-1 --zone=europe-west1-b   # keys handled for you
gcloud compute instances stop web-1 --zone=europe-west1-b
takeaways: Pick machine family by workload; e2 is the cheap default
Use image families to always get the latest patched image
Stopped VMs still pay for disks and static IPs
Spot VMs are cheap but preemptible
pitfalls: Running a database on a Spot VM, or on a VM with a local SSD only, and losing data when it goes away.

quiz.q: You stop a VM for the weekend. What are you still billed for?
options: Its persistent disks (and any reserved static IP)
quiz.explain: Compute charges stop, but storage and reserved addresses keep accruing.

concepts.name: VPC networks and subnets
concepts.summary: Global VPC networks, regional subnets, auto vs custom mode, internal and external IPs, and routes.
concepts.why: Every VM, GKE node and private database address comes from a VPC subnet, so its design is hard to change later.
concepts.body:
A **VPC network** in Google Cloud is **global**: one network spans all regions, and VMs in different regions can talk over internal IPs without VPNs. **Subnets** are **regional** and own a primary IPv4 range (plus optional secondary ranges, used e.g. by GKE Pods and Services).

Two creation modes:

- **Auto mode** creates one subnet per region from a fixed `10.128.0.0/9` block. The `default` network in new projects is auto mode with permissive firewall rules. Fine for experiments.
- **Custom mode** creates no subnets; you add exactly the ranges you plan. Use this for anything real, so ranges do not collide with on-premises or other VPCs you may later connect.

Addresses: each VM NIC gets an **internal IP** from its subnet; an **external IP** is optional (ephemeral or reserved static). VMs without external IPs can still reach the internet through Cloud NAT and Google APIs through Private Google Access.

**Routes** are also global. Every network has system routes for its subnets and a default route `0.0.0.0/0` to the internet gateway; custom routes and Cloud Router (BGP) cover VPNs and interconnects.

A project can hold several VPCs, but they are isolated from each other unless you connect them (peering, VPN, Shared VPC, Network Connectivity Center).
concepts.code:
gcloud compute networks create shop-vpc --subnet-mode=custom

gcloud compute networks subnets create shop-euw1 --network=shop-vpc \
  --region=europe-west1 --range=10.10.0.0/20

gcloud compute networks subnets create shop-use1 --network=shop-vpc \
  --region=us-east1 --range=10.20.0.0/20

gcloud compute networks subnets list --network=shop-vpc
# NAME       REGION        NETWORK   RANGE
# shop-euw1  europe-west1  shop-vpc  10.10.0.0/20
# shop-use1  us-east1      shop-vpc  10.20.0.0/20

gcloud compute routes list --filter="network:shop-vpc" --format="value(destRange,nextHopGateway.basename())"
takeaways: VPC networks and routes are global; subnets are regional
Use custom mode and plan non-overlapping ranges
External IPs are optional; private VMs use NAT and Private Google Access
pitfalls: Building production on the auto-mode default network, whose ranges overlap every other default network you might later peer with.

quiz.q: A VM in us-east1 and one in europe-west1 are in the same VPC. What do they need to talk over internal IPs?
options: Nothing beyond firewall rules allowing it
quiz.explain: A VPC is global, so subnets in different regions are routable to each other; only firewall rules apply.

concepts.name: Firewall rules
concepts.summary: Stateful VPC firewall rules: implied rules, priorities, and targeting by network tag or service account.
concepts.why: Firewall rules are the main network control on VMs and GKE nodes, and most 'cannot connect' problems end here.
concepts.body:
VPC firewall rules are **stateful**: if a connection is allowed in one direction, its return traffic is allowed automatically. Each rule has a direction (`INGRESS` or `EGRESS`), an action (allow or deny), protocols and ports, a source or destination range, a **priority** (0 to 65535, lower wins, default 1000) and a **target**.

Every VPC has two **implied rules** at the lowest priority: deny all ingress and allow all egress. So a new custom VPC accepts no inbound traffic until you add rules.

Targets decide which VMs a rule applies to:

- all instances in the network;
- **network tags** such as `http-server` set on the VM;
- **target service accounts**, which are stronger because changing a VM's service account requires more permission than editing tags.

Useful source ranges to know: `35.235.240.0/20` for Identity-Aware Proxy TCP forwarding (SSH to VMs without external IPs), and `130.211.0.0/22` plus `35.191.0.0/16` for load balancer health checks.

Beyond per-VPC rules, **network firewall policies** and **hierarchical firewall policies** (set at org or folder) let security teams enforce rules across many networks; they are evaluated before the VPC rules. Enable **firewall rules logging** on a rule to see what it allows or denies when debugging.
concepts.code:
# SSH only through IAP, only to VMs tagged ssh
gcloud compute firewall-rules create shop-allow-iap-ssh --network=shop-vpc \
  --direction=INGRESS --action=ALLOW --rules=tcp:22 \
  --source-ranges=35.235.240.0/20 --target-tags=ssh

# HTTP from anywhere to VMs running as the web service account
gcloud compute firewall-rules create shop-allow-http --network=shop-vpc \
  --direction=INGRESS --action=ALLOW --rules=tcp:80,tcp:443 \
  --source-ranges=0.0.0.0/0 \
  --target-service-accounts=web@shop-dev-4821.iam.gserviceaccount.com

# Then connect without an external IP
gcloud compute ssh web-1 --zone=europe-west1-b --tunnel-through-iap
takeaways: Rules are stateful; replies are allowed automatically
Implied rules: deny all ingress, allow all egress
Lower priority number wins
Target by service account for stronger guarantees than tags
pitfalls: Opening tcp:22 from 0.0.0.0/0 instead of using IAP's range.

quiz.q: Two ingress rules match a packet: allow at priority 1000 and deny at priority 900. What happens?
options: Both are logged and the packet is queued
Denied, because 900 is the higher priority
quiz.explain: Lower numbers are higher priority, so the deny at 900 is evaluated first and applies.

concepts.name: Cloud Storage buckets and objects
concepts.summary: Store files as objects in buckets: create buckets, upload and download with gcloud storage, and control access.
concepts.why: Cloud Storage holds everything from user uploads and backups to data lake files and static websites.
concepts.body:
**Cloud Storage** is object storage: you put **objects** (any bytes plus metadata) into **buckets**. Bucket names are globally unique. A bucket has a **location** (region, dual-region or multi-region) chosen at creation and never changed.

There are no real directories: `reports/2026/q3.csv` is one object name, and tools show the `/`-separated prefixes as folders. (Buckets with the optional **hierarchical namespace** do have real folders, useful for analytics workloads.)

Use the `gcloud storage` commands; they replace the older `gsutil` and are faster for large transfers.

Access control:

- Enable **uniform bucket-level access** so only IAM decides access (no per-object ACLs). It is the recommended setting.
- **Public access prevention** blocks `allUsers` grants; many organizations enforce it.
- To share one object temporarily, create a **signed URL** instead of making it public.

Objects are immutable: an upload replaces the whole object. Strong consistency applies: after a successful write, every read and list sees it. Deleted objects are kept for a **soft delete** period (7 days by default) and can be restored, which you pay for as storage.

Upload limits are generous (objects up to 5 TiB), and large files are uploaded in parallel composite or resumable chunks automatically.
concepts.code:
gcloud storage buckets create gs://shop-dev-4821-uploads \
  --location=europe-west1 --uniform-bucket-level-access --public-access-prevention

gcloud storage cp ./report.csv gs://shop-dev-4821-uploads/reports/2026/
gcloud storage ls gs://shop-dev-4821-uploads/reports/
# gs://shop-dev-4821-uploads/reports/2026/

gcloud storage cat gs://shop-dev-4821-uploads/reports/2026/report.csv | head -2
gcloud storage rsync ./site gs://shop-dev-4821-uploads/site --recursive

# Time-limited link without making anything public (needs a signing identity)
gcloud storage sign-url gs://shop-dev-4821-uploads/reports/2026/report.csv --duration=1h \
  --impersonate-service-account=signer@shop-dev-4821.iam.gserviceaccount.com
takeaways: Buckets have a fixed location and a globally unique name
Folders are just name prefixes
Use uniform bucket-level access and IAM; share with signed URLs
Prefer gcloud storage over gsutil
pitfalls: Granting allUsers objectViewer on a bucket to share one file.

quiz.q: How do you rename a 'folder' with 10,000 objects in a standard bucket?
options: Copy every object to the new prefix and delete the old ones
Folders cannot contain that many objects
quiz.explain: Without hierarchical namespace, folders are only prefixes, so a rename rewrites each object.

concepts.name: Cloud Run services
concepts.summary: Deploy a container (or source code) as an autoscaling HTTPS service that scales to zero, and control access, scaling and revisions.
concepts.why: Cloud Run is the quickest path from a container to a production URL, with no servers or clusters to manage.
concepts.body:
**Cloud Run** runs stateless containers. You give it an image; it gives you an HTTPS URL, TLS, autoscaling (including to zero) and per-request or per-instance billing.

The contract for your container: listen on the port in the `PORT` environment variable (8080 by default), respond to HTTP, and keep no state on local disk you need later (the filesystem is in-memory and per instance).

Each deploy creates an immutable **revision**. Traffic can be split between revisions for canaries (`gcloud run services update-traffic --to-revisions=...`) and rolled back instantly.

Settings that matter:

- **Concurrency**: requests per instance (default 80). Lower it for CPU-heavy work.
- **Min/max instances**: `--min-instances=1` removes cold starts; `--max-instances` caps cost and protects your database.
- **CPU and memory**, request **timeout** (default 5 minutes, up to 60).
- **Ingress** (all, internal, internal and load balancer) and **authentication**: by default callers need `roles/run.invoker`; `--allow-unauthenticated` makes it public.
- **Service account** the code runs as (use a dedicated one).

`gcloud run deploy --source .` builds your code with Cloud Build (Dockerfile or buildpacks) and stores the image in Artifact Registry for you. For run-to-completion work use **Cloud Run jobs** instead of services.
concepts.code:
# Dockerfile next to app.py:  FROM python:3.13-slim ... CMD exec gunicorn -b :$PORT app:app
gcloud run deploy orders-api --source . --region=europe-west1 \
  --service-account=orders-api@shop-dev-4821.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --allow-unauthenticated --min-instances=0 --max-instances=20 --concurrency=40
# Service URL: https://orders-api-987654321098.europe-west1.run.app

# Canary: send 10% to the newest revision
gcloud run services update-traffic orders-api --region=europe-west1 \
  --to-revisions=orders-api-00007-xyz=10,orders-api-00006-abc=90

gcloud run services logs read orders-api --region=europe-west1 --limit=20
takeaways: Listen on $PORT and keep instances stateless
Every deploy is a revision; split traffic for canaries
Tune concurrency, min and max instances
Services are private unless you allow unauthenticated access
pitfalls: Doing background work after sending the response with request-based billing, where CPU is throttled outside requests.

quiz.q: Your Cloud Run service returns 403 to browsers right after deploy. Most likely cause?
options: The container is not listening on $PORT
The service requires authentication and allUsers lacks roles/run.invoker
The region does not support HTTPS
quiz.explain: Services require IAM authentication by default; public services need --allow-unauthenticated.

concepts.name: Authentication: ADC and impersonation
concepts.summary: How client libraries find credentials (Application Default Credentials) and how to run local code as a service account without keys.
concepts.why: The same code must authenticate on a laptop, in CI and in production without hard-coded secrets.
concepts.body:
Google client libraries use **Application Default Credentials (ADC)**. They look for credentials in this order:

- the file named by the `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` environment variable;
- the user credentials created by `gcloud auth application-default login` (a file in your gcloud config directory);
- the **metadata server**, available on Compute Engine, GKE, Cloud Run, Cloud Run functions and Cloud Build, which serves tokens for the attached service account.

So code written as `storage.Client()` works everywhere: on your laptop it uses your ADC login, in production the attached service account. Note that `gcloud auth login` (credentials for the CLI) and `gcloud auth application-default login` (credentials for your code) are separate.

To test with exactly production's permissions, **impersonate** the service account instead of downloading a key. You need `roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator` on it; then:

```bash
gcloud auth application-default login --impersonate-service-account=orders-api@shop-dev-4821.iam.gserviceaccount.com
```

The CLI has the same feature per command (`--impersonate-service-account`) or as a config property (`auth/impersonate_service_account`).

Libraries also need a **quota project** for some APIs when using user credentials; `gcloud auth application-default set-quota-project` fixes the related warning.
concepts.code:
# pip install google-cloud-storage
import google.auth
from google.cloud import storage

credentials, project = google.auth.default()
print(type(credentials).__name__, project)
# laptop with ADC login:      Credentials shop-dev-4821
# Cloud Run / GCE / GKE:      Credentials (compute_engine) shop-dev-4821

client = storage.Client()          # same discovery, no key file
for bucket in client.list_buckets(max_results=3):
    print(bucket.name)
takeaways: ADC order: GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS, gcloud ADC file, metadata server
gcloud auth login is for the CLI; application-default login is for your code
Impersonate a service account (Token Creator) instead of using keys
pitfalls: Leaving GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS pointing at an old key file, which silently overrides everything else.

quiz.q: Your code works in Cloud Run but locally fails with 'default credentials not found' even though gcloud commands work. Why?
options: You ran gcloud auth login but not gcloud auth application-default login
Client libraries require a JSON key
quiz.explain: CLI credentials and ADC are stored separately; libraries only read ADC.

concepts.name: Managed instance groups and autoscaling
concepts.summary: Run identical VMs from an instance template with autoscaling, autohealing and rolling updates.
concepts.why: Single VMs are pets; MIGs give you self-healing, scalable fleets that load balancers can target.
concepts.body:
An **instance template** is an immutable description of a VM: machine type, image, disks, metadata, tags, service account. A **managed instance group (MIG)** creates and maintains N identical VMs from a template.

What a MIG does for you:

- **Autoscaling** on CPU utilisation, load balancer serving capacity, Cloud Monitoring metrics or schedules, between a min and max size.
- **Autohealing**: with a health check attached, unhealthy VMs are recreated. Set an initial delay long enough for boot and app start.
- **Regional MIGs** spread VMs across zones of a region, so a zone outage does not take the service down. Prefer them over zonal MIGs for serving.
- **Rolling updates**: point the group at a new template and it replaces VMs gradually, controlled by `--max-surge` and `--max-unavailable`. Canary by updating only a fraction of instances.

Because templates are immutable, a change means a new template (`web-tpl-v2`) and a rolling update. VMs in a MIG should be stateless and configured at boot (startup script, baked image or containers) since any of them can be deleted and recreated at any time.

MIGs are the classic backend for a load balancer. Unmanaged instance groups exist too, but only group existing VMs and offer none of the above.
concepts.code:
gcloud compute instance-templates create web-tpl-v1 \
  --machine-type=e2-small --image-family=debian-12 --image-project=debian-cloud \
  --tags=http-server --metadata-from-file=startup-script=startup.sh

gcloud compute health-checks create http web-hc --port=80 --request-path=/healthz

gcloud compute instance-groups managed create web-mig --region=europe-west1 \
  --template=web-tpl-v1 --size=2 --health-check=web-hc --initial-delay=120

gcloud compute instance-groups managed set-autoscaling web-mig --region=europe-west1 \
  --min-num-replicas=2 --max-num-replicas=10 --target-cpu-utilization=0.6

# Later: roll out a new template with no capacity loss
gcloud compute instance-groups managed rolling-action start-update web-mig \
  --region=europe-west1 --version=template=web-tpl-v2 --max-surge=3 --max-unavailable=0
takeaways: Templates are immutable; change = new template + rolling update
Regional MIGs survive a zone outage
Autohealing needs a health check and a sensible initial delay
pitfalls: Setting the autohealing initial delay shorter than boot time, so VMs are recreated in an endless loop.

quiz.q: How do you change the machine type of every VM in a MIG?
options: Edit the instance template in place
SSH into each VM and resize it
Delete the MIG; resizing is impossible
Create a new template and start a rolling update
quiz.explain: Templates cannot be edited; the MIG rolls VMs over to a new template.

concepts.name: Storage classes, lifecycle and versioning
concepts.summary: Match storage class to access pattern, automate transitions and deletion with lifecycle rules, and protect data with versioning.
concepts.why: Storage bills grow quietly; lifecycle rules and the right class can cut them by an order of magnitude.
concepts.body:
Every object has a **storage class**. All have the same latency and durability; they differ in price per GB, retrieval fee and **minimum storage duration**:

- **Standard**: hot data, no minimum duration.
- **Nearline**: accessed about once a month; 30-day minimum.
- **Coldline**: about once a quarter; 90-day minimum.
- **Archive**: less than once a year; 365-day minimum.

Deleting or rewriting an object before its minimum is billed as if it stayed. Retrieval fees make cold classes expensive to read often.

**Lifecycle rules** act on objects automatically: `SetStorageClass` after N days, `Delete` after N days, delete noncurrent versions, abort incomplete multipart uploads. Rules are evaluated asynchronously, typically within a day. If you cannot predict access patterns, **Autoclass** moves each object between classes based on actual use.

**Object versioning** keeps the previous generation as a noncurrent version when an object is overwritten or deleted. Pair it with a lifecycle rule that deletes old versions, or costs grow forever.

For compliance there are **retention policies** (objects cannot be deleted before an age, optionally locked permanently) and **object holds**. Soft delete protects against accidental deletes even without versioning.
concepts.code:
cat > lifecycle.json <<'EOF'
{"rule": [
  {"action": {"type": "SetStorageClass", "storageClass": "NEARLINE"},
   "condition": {"age": 30, "matchesStorageClass": ["STANDARD"]}},
  {"action": {"type": "SetStorageClass", "storageClass": "ARCHIVE"},
   "condition": {"age": 365}},
  {"action": {"type": "Delete"},
   "condition": {"isLive": false, "numNewerVersions": 3}}
]}
EOF
gcloud storage buckets update gs://shop-dev-4821-uploads \
  --lifecycle-file=lifecycle.json --versioning
gcloud storage buckets describe gs://shop-dev-4821-uploads --format="yaml(lifecycle_config,versioning_enabled)"
takeaways: Same latency in every class; colder = cheaper storage, pricier access, longer minimums
Lifecycle rules automate transitions and deletion
Versioning needs a cleanup rule for noncurrent versions
pitfalls: Moving frequently-read data to Coldline to save money and paying more in retrieval fees.

quiz.q: You upload an object to Archive and delete it after 10 days. How long are you billed for?
quiz.explain: Archive has a 365-day minimum storage duration, charged on early deletion.

concepts.name: Cloud SQL
concepts.summary: Managed PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server: editions, high availability, backups and secure connections.
concepts.why: It is the default home for a relational application database on Google Cloud.
concepts.body:
**Cloud SQL** runs PostgreSQL, MySQL or SQL Server for you: provisioning, patching, backups, replication and failover. You still own schema, queries and sizing.

Key choices at creation:

- **Edition**: Enterprise, or Enterprise Plus with faster machines, a data cache, near-zero-downtime maintenance and higher availability SLA.
- **Machine shape**: vCPUs and memory, plus SSD storage that can grow automatically.
- **Availability type**: `ZONAL`, or `REGIONAL` for **high availability**, a standby in another zone with synchronous disk replication and automatic failover.
- **Connectivity**: private IP (via private services access or PSC) and/or public IP.

Backups: automated daily backups plus **point-in-time recovery** from transaction logs. **Read replicas** (in-region or cross-region) offload reads and serve as disaster-recovery targets. An HA standby is not readable.

Connecting securely: avoid opening public IPs to `0.0.0.0/0`. Use private IP, or the **Cloud SQL Auth Proxy** or language connectors, which authenticate with IAM and encrypt traffic without managing certificates. Cloud Run has built-in support (`--add-cloudsql-instances`) that exposes a Unix socket at `/cloudsql/PROJECT:REGION:INSTANCE`. **IAM database authentication** lets users and service accounts log in without passwords.

When a single instance is no longer enough, look at AlloyDB or Spanner.
concepts.code:
gcloud sql instances create shop-pg --database-version=POSTGRES_17 \
  --edition=ENTERPRISE --cpu=2 --memory=8GiB --region=europe-west1 \
  --availability-type=REGIONAL --enable-point-in-time-recovery
gcloud sql databases create shop --instance=shop-pg
gcloud sql users create app --instance=shop-pg --password="$(openssl rand -base64 24)"

# Local development through the Auth Proxy (uses your ADC credentials)
cloud-sql-proxy shop-dev-4821:europe-west1:shop-pg --port 5432 &
psql "host=127.0.0.1 port=5432 dbname=shop user=app"

# Cloud Run: socket at /cloudsql/shop-dev-4821:europe-west1:shop-pg
gcloud run deploy orders-api --image=IMAGE --region=europe-west1 \
  --add-cloudsql-instances=shop-dev-4821:europe-west1:shop-pg
takeaways: REGIONAL availability = standby in another zone with automatic failover
Enable PITR; add read replicas for reads and DR
Connect via private IP or the Auth Proxy/connectors, not open public IPs
pitfalls: Expecting the HA standby to serve read traffic; use a read replica for that.

quiz.q: What does --availability-type=REGIONAL give you?
options: A readable replica in another region
A standby in another zone with automatic failover
quiz.explain: Cloud SQL HA keeps a synchronous standby in a second zone of the same region and fails over to it.

concepts.name: Cloud Run functions and event triggers
concepts.summary: Deploy single-purpose functions triggered by HTTP or by events from Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub and more via Eventarc.
concepts.why: Functions are the least code needed to react to events, such as processing every uploaded file.
concepts.body:
**Cloud Run functions** (formerly Cloud Functions; the 2nd-generation runtime) let you deploy just a function. Google builds it into a container and runs it on Cloud Run, so you get the same concurrency, scaling and IAM model.

Two signatures, via the **Functions Framework** for your language:

- **HTTP functions** receive a request and return a response.
- **CloudEvent functions** receive an event, such as an object finalized in a bucket or a Pub/Sub message. Event delivery uses **Eventarc**, which supports many Google sources and also Cloud Audit Log events.

Deploy with `gcloud functions deploy` (or `gcloud run deploy --function`). Event functions should be **idempotent**: delivery is at-least-once, and with `--retry` failures are retried until success or the event expires. A bug that always throws will retry for a long time, so log and swallow permanent errors.

```bash
gcloud functions deploy make-thumbnail --gen2 --region=europe-west1 \
  --runtime=python313 --source=. --entry-point=on_upload \
  --trigger-bucket=shop-dev-4821-uploads \
  --service-account=thumbs@shop-dev-4821.iam.gserviceaccount.com
```

Choose a function for small, event-driven glue. When you need several routes, custom system packages or full control of the container, deploy a regular Cloud Run service instead.
takeaways: Cloud Run functions = your function built and run on Cloud Run
HTTP vs CloudEvent signatures; events come through Eventarc
Event handlers must be idempotent and not raise on permanent errors
pitfalls: Writing a thumbnail into the same bucket that triggers the function, creating an infinite loop.

quiz.q: Why must a storage-triggered function be idempotent?
options: Events are delivered at least once and may be retried
quiz.explain: At-least-once delivery means the same event can arrive more than once.

concepts.name: Artifact Registry
concepts.summary: Store container images and language packages in regional repositories, authenticate Docker, and manage access and cleanup.
concepts.why: Every Cloud Run, GKE and Cloud Build workflow pulls images from here.
concepts.body:
**Artifact Registry** hosts container images and packages (npm, Maven, Python, Go, Apt, Yum). It replaces the retired Container Registry (`gcr.io`).

A **repository** has a format (`docker`, `python`, `npm`...) and a location. Image paths look like:

`LOCATION-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT_ID/REPOSITORY/IMAGE:TAG`

Put repositories in the same region as the services that pull from them for speed and to avoid egress.

Authenticate Docker once with `gcloud auth configure-docker LOCATION-docker.pkg.dev`; this installs gcloud as a credential helper. Cloud Build, Cloud Run and GKE use their service accounts, which need `roles/artifactregistry.reader` (pull) or `writer` (push) on the repository or project.

Repository modes:

- **Standard**: your own artifacts.
- **Remote**: a caching proxy of Docker Hub, PyPI, npm and others, shielding you from upstream rate limits and outages.
- **Virtual**: one endpoint that searches several repositories in order.

Useful extras: **cleanup policies** to delete old untagged images automatically, **immutable tags** so `v1.2.0` can never be overwritten, and vulnerability scanning of images. Deploy by **digest** (`@sha256:...`) or immutable tags in production so what runs is exactly what was tested.
concepts.code:
gcloud artifacts repositories create apps --repository-format=docker \
  --location=europe-west1 --immutable-tags --description="Shop images"

gcloud auth configure-docker europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev

IMAGE=europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/shop-dev-4821/apps/orders-api:1.4.0
docker build -t $IMAGE .
docker push $IMAGE

gcloud artifacts docker images list europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/shop-dev-4821/apps --include-tags
takeaways: Image path: LOCATION-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT/REPO/IMAGE:TAG
configure-docker sets up auth for docker push and pull
Use remote repos for upstream caching and cleanup policies for old images
pitfalls: Pushing to gcr.io in new projects; use Artifact Registry paths.

quiz.q: Cloud Run fails to pull an image from another project's repository. What fixes it?
options: Push the image to Docker Hub
Grant roles/artifactregistry.reader to the Cloud Run service agent / deploy identity on that repository
quiz.explain: Pulling needs reader permission on the repository for the identity doing the pull.

concepts.name: Cloud Build CI/CD
concepts.summary: Build, test and deploy with cloudbuild.yaml steps, substitutions and Git-triggered builds running as a dedicated service account.
concepts.why: A managed build that pushes to Artifact Registry and deploys to Cloud Run without any CI servers to run.
concepts.body:
**Cloud Build** runs a sequence of **steps**, each a container image with arguments, in a shared `/workspace` holding your source. A step can be any image: `gcr.io/cloud-builders/docker`, the Cloud SDK image, `node`, `python`, your own test image.

The config file (`cloudbuild.yaml`) lists `steps`, plus options:

- **Substitutions**: built-ins like `$PROJECT_ID`, `$BUILD_ID`, and for Git-triggered builds `$COMMIT_SHA`, `$SHORT_SHA`, `$BRANCH_NAME`. Your own must start with an underscore (`_REGION`).
- `waitFor` to run steps in parallel; `timeout`; `machineType` for bigger workers.
- `images` lists images to push and record in the build's provenance.

Start builds manually with `gcloud builds submit` (uploads the current directory), or create **triggers** that run on pushes or pull requests from GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket via a repository connection.

Builds run as a **service account**; specify a dedicated one rather than relying on defaults. Grant it exactly what the pipeline needs: Artifact Registry Writer, Cloud Run Developer, and Service Account User on the runtime service account it deploys. With a custom service account you must also set a logs destination, e.g. `options.logging: CLOUD_LOGGING_ONLY`.

For private networks, **private pools** run builds on workers peered into your VPC.
concepts.code:
# cloudbuild.yaml (run by a trigger on pushes to main)
steps:
- id: test
  name: python:3.13-slim
  entrypoint: bash
  args: ['-c', 'pip install -r requirements.txt && python -m pytest -q']
- id: build
  name: gcr.io/cloud-builders/docker
  args: ['build', '-t', '${_REPO}/orders-api:$SHORT_SHA', '.']
- id: push
  name: gcr.io/cloud-builders/docker
  args: ['push', '${_REPO}/orders-api:$SHORT_SHA']
- id: deploy
  name: gcr.io/google.com/cloudsdktool/cloud-sdk:slim
  entrypoint: gcloud
  args: ['run', 'deploy', 'orders-api', '--image=${_REPO}/orders-api:$SHORT_SHA', '--region=europe-west1']
substitutions:
  _REPO: europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/shop-dev-4821/apps
options:
  logging: CLOUD_LOGGING_ONLY
takeaways: A build is a list of container steps sharing /workspace
User substitutions start with _; commit variables come from triggers
Run builds as a dedicated, least-privilege service account
pitfalls: Giving the build service account Owner so deploys 'just work'; anyone who can edit the pipeline then owns the project.

quiz.q: Which substitution name is valid for your own variable?
quiz.explain: User-defined substitutions must begin with an underscore.

concepts.name: Pub/Sub messaging
concepts.summary: Decouple services with topics and subscriptions: pull vs push, acknowledgements, retries, dead-letter topics and ordering.
concepts.why: Pub/Sub is the event backbone between services, functions and data pipelines on Google Cloud.
concepts.body:
**Pub/Sub** is a global, serverless messaging service. Publishers send **messages** (bytes plus string attributes) to a **topic**. Each **subscription** on the topic receives its own copy of every message, so you fan out by adding subscriptions.

Subscription types:

- **Pull**: your workers fetch messages, typically with the client library's streaming pull. Best for throughput and control.
- **Push**: Pub/Sub POSTs each message to an HTTPS endpoint, such as a Cloud Run service, optionally with an OIDC token.
- **Export** subscriptions write directly to BigQuery or Cloud Storage.

Delivery is **at-least-once**. A subscriber must **acknowledge** each message within the **ack deadline** (default 10 seconds, extended automatically by client libraries); otherwise it is redelivered. Make handlers idempotent. Unacked messages are retained for 7 days by default.

Reliability features:

- **Dead-letter topics** after N failed delivery attempts (5 to 100), so poison messages stop looping.
- **Retry policy** with exponential backoff.
- **Ordering keys**: messages with the same key are delivered in order (enable on the subscription).
- **Exactly-once delivery** for pull subscriptions in one region, if duplicates are truly unacceptable.
- **Filters** so a subscription only receives messages whose attributes match.

Pub/Sub is not a log you replay from offset 0 by default; for that, enable retention of acknowledged messages and use **seek**, or consider Managed Kafka.
concepts.code:
# pip install google-cloud-pubsub
from concurrent.futures import TimeoutError
from google.cloud import pubsub_v1

project = "shop-dev-4821"
publisher = pubsub_v1.PublisherClient()
topic = publisher.topic_path(project, "orders")
future = publisher.publish(topic, b'{"id": 42}', origin="web")   # attributes as kwargs
print("published", future.result())                              # message ID

subscriber = pubsub_v1.SubscriberClient()
sub = subscriber.subscription_path(project, "orders-worker")

def handle(message):
    print(message.data, message.attributes["origin"])   # b'{"id": 42}' web
    message.ack()                                        # nack()/no ack -> redelivery

streaming = subscriber.subscribe(sub, callback=handle)
with subscriber:
    try:
        streaming.result(timeout=30)
    except TimeoutError:
        streaming.cancel()
        streaming.result()
takeaways: Each subscription gets every message; fan out by adding subscriptions
At-least-once: ack within the deadline and keep handlers idempotent
Use dead-letter topics for poison messages
pitfalls: Acknowledging before processing finishes, so a crash loses the message.

quiz.q: Two worker processes share one pull subscription. How are messages split?
options: Only the first worker receives messages
quiz.explain: Workers on the same subscription share its messages; separate subscriptions each get a full copy.

concepts.name: BigQuery at a glance
concepts.summary: What BigQuery is, how datasets and tables are organised, how you are billed, and how to query and load data from the CLI.
concepts.why: Most analytics, logs and billing data on Google Cloud end up in BigQuery, so every cloud engineer needs the basics.
concepts.body:
**BigQuery** is Google Cloud's serverless data warehouse. There are no clusters to size: you write SQL (GoogleSQL dialect) and it runs on shared compute measured in **slots**. Storage is columnar and separated from compute.

Organisation: project > **dataset** (has a location such as `EU` or `europe-west1`, and IAM) > **table** or view. Refer to tables as `project.dataset.table` in backticks.

Billing has two parts:

- **Storage**, per GB per month, cheaper for data untouched for 90 days.
- **Compute**: either **on-demand**, per TiB scanned (with a monthly free allowance), or **capacity** pricing through editions and slot reservations with autoscaling.

Because on-demand charges by bytes scanned, select only the columns you need (`SELECT *` reads every column), and use **partitioned** and **clustered** tables so filters prune data. `LIMIT` does not reduce bytes scanned. A **dry run** reports bytes before you spend anything.

Data gets in by batch loads from Cloud Storage (free), streaming via the Storage Write API, Pub/Sub BigQuery subscriptions, log sinks and billing export, or federated queries over external tables.

BigQuery is a separate deep topic; this lesson covers what you need as a Google Cloud user.
concepts.code:
# Estimate cost first: dry run reports bytes processed
bq query --use_legacy_sql=false --dry_run \
  'SELECT name, SUM(number) AS total
   FROM `bigquery-public-data.usa_names.usa_1910_current`
   WHERE state = "TX" GROUP BY name ORDER BY total DESC LIMIT 3'
# Query successfully validated. ... this query will process ... bytes of data.

bq mk --dataset --location=EU shop-dev-4821:analytics
bq load --source_format=CSV --autodetect analytics.orders \
  gs://shop-dev-4821-uploads/exports/orders-*.csv
bq query --use_legacy_sql=false 'SELECT COUNT(*) FROM analytics.orders'
takeaways: Serverless: datasets and tables, no clusters
On-demand pricing is per byte scanned; select fewer columns and partition
LIMIT does not reduce cost; dry runs do tell you the cost
pitfalls: Running SELECT * ... LIMIT 10 on a multi-terabyte table to peek at it; use the table preview instead.

quiz.q: Which change reduces on-demand cost for a query on a wide, date-partitioned table?
options: Selecting only needed columns and filtering on the partition column
quiz.explain: Cost is bytes scanned; column pruning and partition filters reduce it, LIMIT does not.

concepts.name: Cloud Logging
concepts.summary: Find logs with the Logging query language, write structured logs, and route them with buckets and sinks.
concepts.why: Logs are the first place you look when anything breaks, and routing them correctly controls cost and retention.
concepts.body:
**Cloud Logging** collects logs from Google Cloud services automatically (Cloud Run, GKE, load balancers, audit logs) and from VMs via the **Ops Agent**. Explore them in **Logs Explorer** or with `gcloud logging read`.

Every entry has a `resource.type` (`cloud_run_revision`, `gce_instance`, `k8s_container`...), a `severity`, a `timestamp`, a `logName` and a payload: `textPayload` or structured `jsonPayload`. The **Logging query language** filters on these: `AND`, `OR`, `NOT`, comparison operators, `:` for "contains" and `=~` for regular expressions.

Write **structured logs**: on Cloud Run, Cloud Run functions and GKE, a single-line JSON object on stdout is parsed into `jsonPayload`, and special fields like `severity` and `message` are understood.

```python
print(json.dumps({"severity": "ERROR", "message": "payment failed", "order_id": 42}))
```

Now you can query `jsonPayload.order_id=42` instead of grepping text.

The **Log Router** sends every entry through **sinks**. By default `_Required` (audit logs, 400 days, free) and `_Default` (everything else, 30 days) **log buckets** receive them. Add sinks to export to BigQuery, Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub or other buckets, and **exclusion filters** to drop noisy logs. Ingestion beyond the free allowance is billed per GiB, so excluding debug noise saves real money.

**Log-based metrics** turn matching entries into Monitoring metrics you can alert on.
concepts.code:
# Errors from one Cloud Run service in the last 6 hours
gcloud logging read '
  resource.type="cloud_run_revision"
  AND resource.labels.service_name="orders-api"
  AND severity>=ERROR' --freshness=6h --limit=20 \
  --format="table(timestamp,severity,jsonPayload.message)"

# Structured field search and regex
gcloud logging read 'jsonPayload.order_id=42 OR textPayload=~"timeout after [0-9]+s"' --limit=5

# Count 5xx responses as a metric you can alert on
gcloud logging metrics create orders_5xx \
  --description="5xx from orders-api" \
  --log-filter='resource.type="cloud_run_revision" AND resource.labels.service_name="orders-api" AND httpRequest.status>=500'
takeaways: Filter on resource.type, severity and payload fields
Log one-line JSON to stdout to get structured jsonPayload
Sinks route logs; exclusions cut ingestion cost
_Required keeps audit logs 400 days, _Default 30 days
pitfalls: Logging multi-line text or stack traces as many entries, which breaks searching and error grouping.

quiz.q: Your Cloud Run app prints Python dicts with print(dict). Why can't you filter on jsonPayload fields?
options: Python repr is not JSON, so it lands in textPayload
quiz.explain: Only valid single-line JSON is parsed into jsonPayload; repr output uses single quotes and is plain text.

concepts.name: Cloud Monitoring and alerting
concepts.summary: Metrics, dashboards, uptime checks and alerting policies with notification channels, plus SLOs.
concepts.why: You want to hear about problems from an alert, not from your users.
concepts.body:
**Cloud Monitoring** stores time series **metrics**. Google services publish hundreds automatically (e.g. `run.googleapis.com/request_count`, `compute.googleapis.com/instance/cpu/utilization`); VMs need the **Ops Agent** for memory and disk metrics; you can add **custom metrics**, **log-based metrics**, and Prometheus metrics via Managed Service for Prometheus. Metrics Explorer and dashboards visualise them; PromQL works in queries.

A metric query has a filter (metric and resource type, labels), an **aligner** that turns raw points into regular intervals per series (`ALIGN_RATE`, `ALIGN_MEAN`, percentiles) and a **reducer** that combines series (`REDUCE_SUM` across all revisions).

An **alerting policy** contains one or more conditions (threshold, metric absence, or a PromQL or log match) and **notification channels**: email, SMS, Slack, PagerDuty, webhooks, Pub/Sub. The condition's **duration** avoids alerting on a single spike.

**Uptime checks** probe HTTP(S) or TCP endpoints from several regions worldwide and can alert when a site is down from the outside.

Mature teams alert on **SLOs** rather than raw CPU: define a service-level indicator (fraction of good requests, latency under a threshold), a target such as 99.9% over 28 days, and alert on **burn rate**, i.e. how fast the error budget is being spent.
concepts.code:
cat > policy.yaml <<'EOF'
displayName: orders-api 5xx rate
combiner: OR
conditions:
- displayName: 5xx above 1 per second for 5 minutes
  conditionThreshold:
    filter: >-
      resource.type = "cloud_run_revision" AND
      resource.labels.service_name = "orders-api" AND
      metric.type = "run.googleapis.com/request_count" AND
      metric.labels.response_code_class = "5xx"
    aggregations:
    - {alignmentPeriod: 60s, perSeriesAligner: ALIGN_RATE, crossSeriesReducer: REDUCE_SUM}
    comparison: COMPARISON_GT
    thresholdValue: 1
    duration: 300s
notificationChannels: [projects/shop-dev-4821/notificationChannels/1234567890]
EOF
gcloud monitoring policies create --policy-from-file=policy.yaml
takeaways: Aligners regularise each series; reducers combine series
Alerts = conditions + duration + notification channels
Uptime checks test from outside; SLO burn-rate alerts beat CPU alerts
pitfalls: Alerting on every CPU spike with no duration, which trains everyone to ignore alerts.

quiz.q: In an alert condition, what does a duration of 300s do?
options: Requires the condition to hold for 5 minutes before firing
Keeps the incident open for 5 minutes
Delays notifications by 5 minutes after firing
quiz.explain: The condition must be continuously true for the duration, filtering out brief spikes.

concepts.name: Secret Manager
concepts.summary: Store API keys and passwords as versioned secrets, grant access per secret, and inject them into Cloud Run and code.
concepts.why: Secrets in environment files, images or Git leak; Secret Manager gives versioning, IAM and audit logs instead.
concepts.body:
**Secret Manager** stores small sensitive values (up to 64 KiB) as **secrets** with immutable **versions**. Adding a new value creates version 2; the alias `latest` points to the newest enabled version. Versions can be disabled (reversible) or destroyed (permanent).

Access control is per secret: grant `roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor` on that secret to the service account that needs it, not on the whole project. Every access is recorded in Data Access audit logs if you enable them.

Ways to consume a secret:

- **Cloud Run / Cloud Run functions**: `--set-secrets=ENV_VAR=secret:version` exposes it as an environment variable, or `/path=secret:latest` mounts it as a file. Mounted `latest` picks up new versions on read; environment variables are resolved at instance start.
- **Client library**: `access_secret_version("projects/P/secrets/S/versions/latest")`.
- **GKE**: the Secret Manager add-on (CSI driver) mounts secrets as files.

Pin a specific version (e.g. `:3`) in production so a rotation is a deliberate deploy, or use `latest` with file mounts if the app re-reads it. Use **rotation schedules**, which publish notifications to Pub/Sub so your code can rotate the value. Replication is automatic (Google-chosen regions) or user-managed when data residency matters; regional secrets are also available.
concepts.code:
printf 's3cr3t-p4ss' | gcloud secrets create db-pass --data-file=- --replication-policy=automatic
printf 'n3w-p4ss' | gcloud secrets versions add db-pass --data-file=-   # version 2

gcloud secrets add-iam-policy-binding db-pass \
  --member="serviceAccount:orders-api@shop-dev-4821.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \
  --role="roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor"

gcloud secrets versions access latest --secret=db-pass     # n3w-p4ss

# Env var pinned to version 2, plus a file mount that follows latest
gcloud run services update orders-api --region=europe-west1 \
  --set-secrets=DB_PASS=db-pass:2,/secrets/api-key=api-key:latest
takeaways: Secrets have immutable versions; latest is an alias
Grant secretAccessor on individual secrets
Cloud Run can inject secrets as env vars or files
pitfalls: Passing a secret with --set-env-vars, which stores it in plain text in the service config.

quiz.q: You add a new version of a secret used as DB_PASS=db-pass:latest env var in Cloud Run. When does the service see it?
options: Never; env vars must pin a number
When new instances start (e.g. after a new revision deploy)
quiz.explain: Environment variable secrets are resolved when an instance starts.

concepts.name: Cloud Load Balancing and Cloud CDN
concepts.summary: Choose between Application and Network load balancers, wire forwarding rule to backends, and cache at the edge with Cloud CDN.
concepts.why: A global load balancer gives one anycast IP, managed TLS, autoscaled backends in many regions and an edge cache.
concepts.code:
# Global HTTPS load balancer with CDN in front of a Cloud Run service
gcloud compute network-endpoint-groups create api-neg --region=europe-west1 \
  --network-endpoint-type=serverless --cloud-run-service=orders-api
gcloud compute backend-services create api-be --global \
  --load-balancing-scheme=EXTERNAL_MANAGED --enable-cdn
gcloud compute backend-services add-backend api-be --global \
  --network-endpoint-group=api-neg --network-endpoint-group-region=europe-west1
gcloud compute url-maps create api-map --default-service=api-be
gcloud compute ssl-certificates create api-cert --domains=api.example.com --global
gcloud compute target-https-proxies create api-proxy --url-map=api-map --ssl-certificates=api-cert
gcloud compute addresses create api-ip --global
gcloud compute forwarding-rules create api-fr --global --load-balancing-scheme=EXTERNAL_MANAGED \
  --address=api-ip --target-https-proxy=api-proxy --ports=443
takeaways: Forwarding rule -> proxy -> URL map -> backend service -> backends
Serverless NEGs put Cloud Run behind a load balancer
CDN is enabled per backend service; choose the cache mode deliberately
pitfalls: Forgetting the health-check firewall ranges, so every VM backend shows unhealthy.
Using FORCE_CACHE_ALL on responses that contain per-user data.

quiz.q: Which resource decides that /images/* goes to a bucket and everything else to Cloud Run?
quiz.explain: Host and path routing lives in the URL map, which picks a backend service or bucket.

concepts.name: Private connectivity: NAT, PGA, Shared VPC
concepts.summary: Keep workloads off the public internet with Cloud NAT, Private Google Access, private service access, Shared VPC and Private Service Connect.
concepts.why: Production designs remove external IPs; you then need these pieces for outbound traffic, Google APIs and managed services.
concepts.body:
Once VMs, GKE nodes and serverless egress have no external IPs, several services fill the gaps:

- **Cloud NAT**: managed outbound NAT per region, configured on a **Cloud Router**. Private VMs can download packages and call third-party APIs; nothing can connect in.
- **Private Google Access** (a subnet flag): private VMs reach Google APIs such as Cloud Storage without NAT.
- **Private services access**: a VPC peering to a Google-managed network, used to give Cloud SQL, AlloyDB or Memorystore a private IP in your address space. You reserve an IP range for it.
- **Private Service Connect (PSC)**: expose a service as an endpoint IP inside a consumer VPC, for Google APIs or for services published by another team or vendor. Unlike peering, it does not merge address spaces.
- **Direct VPC egress** (or Serverless VPC Access connectors) lets Cloud Run send traffic into a VPC.

To share one network across many projects, use **Shared VPC**: a **host project** owns the VPC and subnets; **service projects** create VMs and services in those subnets. Network admins control IPs and firewalls centrally while app teams own their projects; grant `roles/compute.networkUser` per subnet.

**VPC Network Peering** connects two VPCs privately but is **non-transitive**: if A peers with B and B with C, A cannot reach C.
concepts.code:
# Outbound internet for private VMs in europe-west1
gcloud compute routers create shop-router --network=shop-vpc --region=europe-west1
gcloud compute routers nats create shop-nat --router=shop-router --region=europe-west1 \
  --auto-allocate-nat-external-ips --nat-all-subnet-ip-ranges

# Google APIs without NAT
gcloud compute networks subnets update shop-euw1 --region=europe-west1 \
  --enable-private-ip-google-access

# Private IP range for managed services (Cloud SQL, AlloyDB...)
gcloud compute addresses create google-managed --global --purpose=VPC_PEERING \
  --prefix-length=16 --network=shop-vpc
gcloud services vpc-peerings connect --service=servicenetworking.googleapis.com \
  --ranges=google-managed --network=shop-vpc
takeaways: Cloud NAT gives outbound-only internet to private workloads
Private Google Access is a subnet setting for Google APIs
Shared VPC: central host project, app teams in service projects
Peering is non-transitive; PSC avoids merging address spaces
pitfalls: Expecting traffic to flow A to C through a shared peered VPC B.

quiz.q: Private VMs need to pull packages from the internet but must not be reachable from it. What do you add?
options: An external IP per VM with a deny-ingress rule
Cloud NAT on a Cloud Router
quiz.explain: Cloud NAT provides outbound-only translation; PGA only covers Google APIs.

concepts.name: Choosing a database: Firestore to Spanner
concepts.summary: When to pick Firestore, Bigtable, Spanner, AlloyDB, Cloud SQL, Memorystore or BigQuery, by data model, scale and consistency needs.
concepts.why: Picking the wrong database is the most expensive architectural mistake to undo.
concepts.body:
Google Cloud offers a database for most shapes of data. A practical map:

- **Cloud SQL**: managed PostgreSQL/MySQL/SQL Server on one primary. Default for typical OLTP apps.
- **AlloyDB for PostgreSQL**: PostgreSQL-compatible with a disaggregated storage layer, faster transactions, read pool instances and a **columnar engine** for analytical queries. For demanding Postgres workloads.
- **Spanner**: relational, SQL, strongly consistent, scaling writes horizontally across nodes and regions, with up to 99.999% availability in multi-region configs. For global or very large OLTP that outgrows one primary.
- **Firestore**: serverless document database (collections of JSON-like documents), strongly consistent, with real-time listeners and offline mobile/web SDKs. Pay per operation; great for app backends.
- **Bigtable**: wide-column NoSQL for huge throughput at single-digit millisecond latency: time series, IoT, ad tech. Access by row key only.
- **Memorystore**: managed Valkey, Redis and Memcached for caching.
- **BigQuery**: analytics warehouse, not an OLTP store.

Questions to ask: Do I need joins and multi-row transactions (relational)? How big will writes get? Is global distribution required? What access patterns exist (key lookups, ranges, ad-hoc analytics)? Is per-operation or per-node pricing better at my traffic?
concepts.code:
# pip install google-cloud-firestore
from google.cloud import firestore

db = firestore.Client(project="shop-dev-4821")
users = db.collection("users")
users.document("ada").set({"name": "Ada", "plan": "pro", "age": 36})
users.document("bob").set({"name": "Bob", "plan": "free", "age": 29})

query = users.where(filter=firestore.FieldFilter("plan", "==", "pro"))
for doc in query.stream():
    print(doc.id, doc.to_dict()["name"])
# ada Ada

# Listen for live changes (real-time updates)
watch = users.document("ada").on_snapshot(lambda docs, changes, ts: print(docs[0].to_dict()))
takeaways: Cloud SQL by default; AlloyDB for heavy Postgres; Spanner when one primary is not enough
Firestore for serverless app documents with real-time sync
Bigtable for massive key-range workloads; BigQuery for analytics
pitfalls: Choosing Spanner or Bigtable for a small app and paying for capacity it never uses.

quiz.q: A global payments system needs relational schema, strong consistency and writes beyond one machine. Which fits?
quiz.explain: Spanner is the horizontally scalable, strongly consistent relational database.

concepts.name: Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)
concepts.summary: Run Kubernetes on Google Cloud: Autopilot vs Standard clusters, release channels, VPC-native networking and exposing workloads.
concepts.why: GKE is the platform for many-service systems that need Kubernetes' scheduling, ecosystem and portability.
concepts.body:
**GKE** runs the Kubernetes control plane for you. Two modes:

- **Autopilot**: Google also manages nodes. You deploy Pods; you pay for the CPU, memory and storage your Pods request. Security hardening and Workload Identity are on by default. The recommended default.
- **Standard**: you manage **node pools** (machine types, autoscaling, Spot nodes, GPUs) and pay for the nodes, used or not. Needed for privileged workloads or very custom node setups.

Clusters are **regional** (control plane and nodes across three zones) or zonal; use regional for production. Enrol in a **release channel** (Rapid, Regular, Stable, Extended) so control plane and nodes are upgraded automatically, and use maintenance windows and exclusions to control when.

Networking is **VPC-native**: Pods and Services get IPs from subnet secondary ranges, so Pods are directly routable in the VPC. A `Service` of type `LoadBalancer` creates a passthrough Network Load Balancer; a **Gateway** or Ingress creates an Application Load Balancer that can send traffic straight to Pods via NEGs.

Access uses `gcloud container clusters get-credentials`, which writes a kubeconfig that authenticates through the `gke-gcloud-auth-plugin`. Cluster access is controlled by both IAM (e.g. `roles/container.developer`) and Kubernetes RBAC.

Compare with Cloud Run before choosing: GKE gives control and ecosystem at the price of operating Kubernetes.
concepts.code:
gcloud container clusters create-auto shop-gke --region=europe-west1 \
  --network=shop-vpc --subnetwork=shop-euw1 --release-channel=regular
gcloud container clusters get-credentials shop-gke --region=europe-west1

kubectl create deployment orders \
  --image=europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/shop-dev-4821/apps/orders-api:1.4.0
kubectl set resources deployment orders --requests=cpu=250m,memory=512Mi
kubectl expose deployment orders --type=LoadBalancer --port=80 --target-port=8080
kubectl get service orders
# NAME     TYPE           CLUSTER-IP     EXTERNAL-IP    PORT(S)
# orders   LoadBalancer   34.118.x.x     35.205.x.x     80:31234/TCP
takeaways: Autopilot: pay per Pod request, nodes managed; Standard: you manage node pools
Regional clusters plus a release channel for production
VPC-native: Pods get routable VPC IPs from secondary ranges
pitfalls: Omitting resource requests on Autopilot and getting small defaults that throttle the app.

quiz.q: In Autopilot, what mainly drives the compute bill?
quiz.explain: Autopilot bills for the CPU, memory and storage that Pods request.

concepts.name: Cloud KMS and customer-managed keys
concepts.summary: Key rings, keys and versions in Cloud KMS, envelope encryption, CMEK for Google services, and HSM or external keys.
concepts.why: Regulated workloads must control, rotate and be able to revoke the keys that protect their data.
concepts.body:
Google encrypts all data at rest by default with Google-managed keys. **Cloud KMS** lets you hold the keys yourself.

Structure: a **key ring** (in a location, cannot be deleted) contains **keys**; each key has **versions**. A key has a purpose: symmetric encryption, asymmetric encryption or signing, or MAC. Encryption uses the primary version; decryption works with any enabled version, so **automatic rotation** (e.g. every 90 days) is painless. Destroying a version is scheduled, by default 30 days later, giving time to undo a mistake.

Protection levels: **software**, **HSM** (Cloud HSM, FIPS 140-2 Level 3), or **external** (Cloud EKM, the key stays in a partner key manager outside Google).

Two ways to use KMS:

- **Envelope encryption** in your code: generate a data key locally, encrypt data with it, and encrypt (wrap) the data key with KMS. Direct `encrypt` calls are limited to 64 KiB of plaintext.
- **CMEK** (customer-managed encryption keys): configure Cloud Storage, BigQuery, Cloud SQL, Pub/Sub, GKE and others to protect data with your key. Grant the service's **service agent** `roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter` on the key. Disabling the key makes the data unreadable: a powerful kill switch and an outage risk.

Separate duties: key administrators (`cloudkms.admin`) should not also be the ones who can decrypt.
concepts.code:
gcloud kms keyrings create shop-ring --location=europe-west1
gcloud kms keys create storage-key --keyring=shop-ring --location=europe-west1 \
  --purpose=encryption --rotation-period=90d --next-rotation-time=2026-12-01T00:00:00Z

# Direct encrypt/decrypt (small payloads only)
echo -n "card-token-123" > plain.txt
gcloud kms encrypt --key=storage-key --keyring=shop-ring --location=europe-west1 \
  --plaintext-file=plain.txt --ciphertext-file=secret.enc
gcloud kms decrypt --key=storage-key --keyring=shop-ring --location=europe-west1 \
  --ciphertext-file=secret.enc --plaintext-file=-          # card-token-123

# CMEK: let Cloud Storage's service agent use the key, then set it as bucket default
gcloud storage service-agent --project=shop-dev-4821 --authorize-cmek=\
projects/shop-dev-4821/locations/europe-west1/keyRings/shop-ring/cryptoKeys/storage-key
gcloud storage buckets update gs://shop-dev-4821-uploads --default-encryption-key=\
