projects/shop-dev-4821/locations/europe-west1/keyRings/shop-ring/cryptoKeys/storage-key
takeaways: Key ring > key > versions; rotation keeps old versions for decryption
Use envelope encryption for data; KMS wraps the data key
CMEK needs the service agent to have encrypter/decrypter on the key
pitfalls: Disabling or destroying a CMEK key without realising every dataset using it becomes unreadable.

quiz.q: After automatic rotation, what happens to data encrypted with the old key version?
options: It can still be decrypted because the old version stays enabled
It is moved to Archive storage
quiz.explain: Rotation only changes the primary version for new encryptions; older versions remain usable for decryption.

concepts.name: Infrastructure as code with Terraform
concepts.summary: Manage Google Cloud resources declaratively with the Terraform google provider, remote state in Cloud Storage and service account impersonation.
concepts.why: Clicking and ad-hoc gcloud do not scale; IaC makes environments reviewable, reproducible and recoverable.
concepts.body:
**Terraform** (HashiCorp, or the open-source fork OpenTofu) is the most common way to manage Google Cloud infrastructure as code. You declare resources in `.tf` files; `terraform plan` shows the diff against reality; `terraform apply` makes it so.

Google Cloud specifics:

- The `google` provider (and `google-beta` for preview features) authenticates with ADC. Set `impersonate_service_account` so humans and CI apply as one controlled service account instead of their own broad rights.
- Store **state** remotely in a Cloud Storage bucket with the `gcs` backend; it supports locking. Enable object versioning on that bucket, and treat state as sensitive: it can contain secrets.
- Enable APIs as resources (`google_project_service`) so a fresh project bootstraps itself.
- IAM has three resource styles: `_iam_policy` (authoritative for the whole resource, dangerous), `_iam_binding` (authoritative for one role) and `_iam_member` (adds one member, safest to mix with other tools).

Google's **Cloud Foundation Fabric** and **Terraform blueprints** provide vetted modules for projects, VPCs and landing zones. **Infrastructure Manager** runs Terraform as a managed service; the older Deployment Manager is deprecated.

Run Terraform from CI (e.g. Cloud Build or GitHub Actions with Workload Identity Federation) after code review, not from laptops.
takeaways: plan shows the diff; apply makes it real
Remote state in a versioned GCS bucket; it is sensitive
Apply via an impersonated service account from CI
Prefer _iam_member over authoritative _iam_policy
pitfalls: Using google_project_iam_policy, which silently removes every binding not listed, including Google service agents.

quiz.q: Which IAM resource type is safest when other tools also grant roles on the same project?
quiz.explain: _iam_member only adds one member to one role and leaves other bindings alone.

concepts.name: Vertex AI overview
concepts.summary: Google Cloud's AI platform: Gemini and Model Garden models, custom training, endpoints, pipelines and the Gen AI SDK.
concepts.why: Generative AI and ML features in Google Cloud apps are built on Vertex AI's models, endpoints and governance.
concepts.body:
**Vertex AI** groups Google Cloud's machine learning services under one API, IAM model and set of quotas.

The main pieces:

- **Generative models**: Gemini models, plus partner and open models in **Model Garden**. Call them through the **Google Gen AI SDK** (`google-genai`) with `vertexai=True`; requests are billed to your project and governed by its IAM, VPC Service Controls and data residency settings.
- **Agent tooling**: grounding with Google Search or your own data, function calling, and RAG and agent services for building assistants.
- **Custom training**: run your training container or script on managed CPUs, GPUs or TPUs (custom jobs, hyperparameter tuning).
- **Model Registry** and **endpoints**: version models and deploy them for online prediction with autoscaling, or run **batch prediction** over files in Cloud Storage or tables in BigQuery.
- **Vertex AI Pipelines** (Kubeflow Pipelines) for reproducible ML workflows, and **Workbench** notebooks.

Access is controlled by roles such as `roles/aiplatform.user`. Generative model availability and quotas vary by region; the `global` location routes to available capacity. Model IDs change frequently as versions are released and retired, so pin a current one deliberately and watch deprecation notices.
concepts.code:
# pip install google-genai   (uses ADC; needs roles/aiplatform.user)
from google import genai

client = genai.Client(vertexai=True, project="shop-dev-4821", location="global")
MODEL = "gemini-2.5-flash"     # pick a current model ID from Model Garden

resp = client.models.generate_content(
    model=MODEL,
    contents="Write a one-line product description for a waterproof hiking boot.",
)
print(resp.text)
# Waterproof, grippy and light: the boot that keeps going when the trail doesn't.
print(resp.usage_metadata.total_token_count)   # billed tokens, e.g. 41
takeaways: Vertex AI = models, training, endpoints and pipelines under one project's IAM and billing
Use the Gen AI SDK with vertexai=True for Gemini on Google Cloud
Model IDs and regional availability change; pin and monitor them
pitfalls: Hard-coding a preview model ID in production and breaking when it is retired.

quiz.q: What does vertexai=True change when using the Gen AI SDK?
options: Requests go to Vertex AI in your project, using ADC, IAM and project billing
It switches to a smaller model
quiz.explain: With vertexai=True the client calls the Vertex AI API under your Google Cloud project.

concepts.name: Cost management and optimisation
concepts.summary: Budgets and alerts, billing export to BigQuery, labels for attribution, committed use and Spot discounts, and recommenders.
concepts.why: Cloud costs scale with usage and mistakes; visibility and the right discounts often save 30% or more.
concepts.body:
Cost control is visibility first, then discounts, then architecture.

Visibility:

- **Budgets** on a billing account, optionally scoped to projects, services or labels, send alerts at thresholds of actual or **forecasted** spend. They do not stop spending; for a hard stop you would wire the budget's Pub/Sub notifications to automation.
- **Billing export to BigQuery** gives line-item costs (standard or detailed per-resource), queryable with SQL and connectable to dashboards.
- **Labels** (`team=checkout`, `env=prod`) on resources flow into the export, enabling chargeback. Agree on a label scheme early and enforce it in Terraform.

Discounts:

- **Committed use discounts**: commit to resources or spend for 1 or 3 years for large savings on steady workloads (Compute Engine, Cloud SQL, Cloud Run, GKE and more).
- **Sustained use discounts** apply automatically to some VM families that run most of the month.
- **Spot VMs** and Spot GKE nodes for interruptible work.

Waste: the **Recommender** flags idle VMs, oversized machines, unattached disks and unused IPs. Common leaks are forgotten static IPs and disks, log ingestion, BigQuery `SELECT *`, cross-region egress, and non-zero min instances on idle services.

Review cost weekly per project and label; surprises found in a week are cheap.
concepts.code:
gcloud billing budgets create --billing-account=01AB23-45CD67-89EF01 \
  --display-name="shop-prod monthly" --budget-amount=2000USD \
  --filter-projects=projects/shop-prod-1234 \
  --threshold-rule=percent=0.5 --threshold-rule=percent=0.9 \
  --threshold-rule=percent=1.0,basis=forecasted-spend

# Top services last month from the standard billing export
bq query --use_legacy_sql=false '
SELECT service.description AS service,
       ROUND(SUM(cost) + SUM(IFNULL((SELECT SUM(c.amount) FROM UNNEST(credits) c), 0)), 2) AS net
FROM `shop-billing.billing_export.gcp_billing_export_v1_01AB23_45CD67_89EF01`
WHERE invoice.month = "202609"
GROUP BY service ORDER BY net DESC LIMIT 5'
takeaways: Budgets alert; they do not cap spend
Billing export + labels = cost per team and environment
CUDs for steady load, Spot for interruptible, Recommender for waste
pitfalls: Creating a budget and assuming it will stop a runaway workload.

quiz.q: Spend jumps and the budget hits 100%. What happens by default?
options: Alerts are sent; resources keep running and billing continues
quiz.explain: Budgets only notify unless you build automation on their Pub/Sub notifications.

concepts.name: IAM at scale: conditions, deny, federation
concepts.summary: Custom roles, IAM Conditions, deny policies, Workload Identity Federation for external workloads, and analysing effective access.
concepts.why: Large organizations need time-bound, attribute-based and keyless access that basic allow policies cannot express.
concepts.body:
Beyond plain role bindings, IAM has several precision tools.

**Custom roles** bundle exactly the permissions you need, at org or project level. They need maintenance as services add permissions, so use them where predefined roles are clearly too broad.

**IAM Conditions** attach a CEL expression to a binding. Common uses: temporary access (`request.time < timestamp(...)`), limiting to resources by name prefix (`resource.name.startsWith(...)`) or by **tags**. Not every resource type supports every attribute, so test conditions.

**Deny policies** are evaluated before allow policies and win: deny specific permissions to a principal set, with exceptions, attached at org, folder or project. Use them for hard guardrails such as "nobody except the security group can create service account keys". They use the `service.googleapis.com/resource.verb` permission format.

**Workload Identity Federation** lets workloads outside Google Cloud (GitHub Actions, GitLab, AWS, Azure, Kubernetes, any OIDC or SAML IdP) exchange their own token for short-lived Google credentials. No keys. Always set an **attribute condition** that pins the trusted repository or account; an open provider would trust every GitHub user.

Analysis: **Policy Analyzer** answers "who can access X", **Policy Troubleshooter** explains a denial, and **role recommendations** remove unused permissions from over-granted principals. **Privileged Access Manager** provides just-in-time, approved elevation.
concepts.code:
# Temporary, conditional access that expires by itself
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding shop-prod-1234 \
  --member="user:contractor@example.com" --role="roles/logging.viewer" \
  --condition='expression=request.time < timestamp("2026-12-31T00:00:00Z"),title=until-2027'

# Keyless deploys from GitHub Actions
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools create github --location=global
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers create-oidc shop-repo --location=global \
  --workload-identity-pool=github --issuer-uri="https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com" \
  --attribute-mapping="google.subject=assertion.sub,attribute.repository=assertion.repository" \
  --attribute-condition="assertion.repository == 'example-org/shop'"

gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding deployer@shop-prod-1234.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --role=roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser \
  --member="principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/projects/111122223333/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/github/attribute.repository/example-org/shop"
takeaways: Conditions add CEL constraints (time, resource name, tags) to a binding
Deny policies override allows; use them for hard guardrails
Workload Identity Federation replaces keys for external workloads; always set an attribute condition
pitfalls: Creating a GitHub OIDC provider without an attribute condition, letting any repository impersonate your service account if other bindings are loose.

quiz.q: A user has Owner via an allow policy and a deny policy denies iam.googleapis.com/serviceAccountKeys.create to all users. Can they create a key?
options: No, deny policies are evaluated first and win
Only if the condition is time-bound
quiz.explain: Deny rules are checked before allow policies; a matching deny blocks the permission regardless of roles.

concepts.name: Organization Policy Service
concepts.summary: Guardrails that restrict how resources may be configured: list and boolean constraints, custom constraints, inheritance and dry run.
concepts.why: IAM decides who may act; org policies decide what configurations are allowed at all, for everyone.
concepts.body:
The **Organization Policy Service** sets **constraints** on resource configuration across the hierarchy. Where IAM says "Alice may create buckets", org policy says "no bucket anywhere may be public" or "resources may only be created in EU locations", even for Owners.

Constraint types:

- **Boolean**: on or off, e.g. `iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation`, `storage.publicAccessPrevention`, `compute.requireOsLogin`, `sql.restrictPublicIp`.
- **List**: allowed or denied values, e.g. `gcp.resourceLocations` (with value groups like `in:eu-locations`), `compute.vmExternalIpAccess`, `iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains` (domain-restricted sharing).
- **Custom constraints**: your own rules as CEL conditions on resource fields for supported services, e.g. "GKE clusters must enable Workload Identity". Google's newer **managed constraints** are built on the same engine.

Policies are set on org, folder or project and **inherited**. A child can replace or, for list constraints, merge with the parent (`inheritFromParent`). **Tags** let you apply conditional rules ("enforce unless tagged `env=sandbox`").

Org policies apply on **create or update**; existing non-compliant resources are not changed. Roll out safely with a **dry-run** spec, which logs would-be violations without enforcing, then enforce. Managing policies needs `roles/orgpolicy.policyAdmin`, usually granted only at the org level. Newer organizations get a set of secure-by-default constraints enforced automatically.
concepts.code:
cat > locations.yaml <<'EOF'
name: folders/123456789012/policies/gcp.resourceLocations
spec:
  rules:
  - values:
      allowedValues:
      - in:eu-locations
EOF
gcloud org-policies set-policy locations.yaml

cat > no-keys.yaml <<'EOF'
name: organizations/555555555555/policies/iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation
spec:
  rules:
  - enforce: true
EOF
gcloud org-policies set-policy no-keys.yaml

# What actually applies to a project after inheritance?
gcloud org-policies describe gcp.resourceLocations --project=shop-dev-4821 --effective
takeaways: Org policy constrains configuration for everyone; IAM grants actions to someone
Boolean, list and custom (CEL) constraints, inherited down the tree
Only new creates/updates are checked; use dry run before enforcing
pitfalls: Enforcing a location or domain restriction org-wide without dry run and breaking deployments that depend on global resources.

quiz.q: gcp.resourceLocations allows only EU locations on a folder. A project Owner in that folder creates a VM in us-east1. What happens?
options: It succeeds because Owner has every permission
It succeeds and an alert is sent
It succeeds but is moved to the EU
It is denied: org policy constraints apply regardless of IAM roles
quiz.explain: Org policies restrict allowed configurations for everyone; IAM roles cannot override them.

concepts.name: VPC Service Controls
concepts.summary: Service perimeters that block data exfiltration through Google APIs, with access levels, ingress/egress rules and dry-run rollout.
concepts.why: IAM cannot stop a valid credential from copying data to an outside project; perimeters can.
concepts.body:
IAM answers who may call an API. **VPC Service Controls (VPC SC)** adds where data may go. A **service perimeter** surrounds a set of projects and a list of **restricted services** (e.g. `storage.googleapis.com`, `bigquery.googleapis.com`). Calls to those services are allowed only when both the caller's context and the target resources are inside the perimeter.

That blocks classic exfiltration paths: a stolen credential used from the internet, copying a bucket to an attacker's project, or a BigQuery query writing to an outside dataset. Violations fail with an error mentioning `vpcServiceControlsUniqueIdentifier` and are logged as Policy Denied audit logs.

Building blocks, managed through **Access Context Manager** in an org-level access policy:

- **Access levels**: conditions on IP ranges, device posture or identities that may enter from outside.
- **Ingress and egress rules**: precise exceptions (this service account may read from that external project's bucket).
- **Perimeter bridges** for sharing between perimeters; **restricted.googleapis.com** VIP plus DNS so VPC traffic stays on the restricted endpoint.

Rollout is the hard part. Many workflows touch services across projects (Cloud Build, logging sinks, Marketplace, third-party SaaS). Always start with a **dry-run** perimeter, study the dry-run violation logs for weeks, add ingress/egress rules, then enforce. VPC SC complements IAM and org policy; it does not replace them.
concepts.code:
POLICY=$(gcloud access-context-manager policies list --organization=555555555555 --format="value(name)")

# 1. Dry run: log violations without blocking anything
gcloud access-context-manager perimeters dry-run create shop_data --policy=$POLICY \
  --perimeter-title="Shop data" --perimeter-type=regular \
  --perimeter-resources=projects/987654321098,projects/444455556666 \
  --perimeter-restricted-services=storage.googleapis.com,bigquery.googleapis.com

# 2. Review would-be denials
gcloud logging read 'protoPayload.metadata.dryRun="true" AND
  protoPayload.metadata."@type"="type.googleapis.com/google.cloud.audit.VpcServiceControlAuditMetadata"' \
  --project=shop-dev-4821 --freshness=7d --limit=20

# 3. Enforce once clean
gcloud access-context-manager perimeters dry-run enforce shop_data --policy=$POLICY
takeaways: Perimeters restrict Google API data flows across a project boundary
Access levels and ingress/egress rules are the controlled exceptions
Always roll out in dry-run mode first
pitfalls: Enforcing a perimeter directly and breaking CI, log sinks and cross-project jobs you did not know existed.

quiz.q: An insider with valid read access copies a protected bucket to their personal project. Which control blocks it?
options: A VPC Service Controls perimeter around the data project
quiz.explain: The copy is authorised by IAM, but the destination is outside the perimeter, so VPC SC denies it.

concepts.name: Audit logs and org-wide log sinks
concepts.summary: Which Cloud Audit Logs exist and are on by default, enabling Data Access logs, and centralising logs with aggregated sinks.
concepts.why: Incident response and compliance depend on knowing who did what, where, and having that record outside the reach of attackers.
concepts.body:
**Cloud Audit Logs** record API activity on Google Cloud resources. Four types:

- **Admin Activity**: configuration and metadata changes (create VM, set IAM policy). Always on, free, cannot be disabled; kept 400 days in `_Required`.
- **Data Access**: reads of configuration and reads or writes of user data. **Off by default** for most services (BigQuery is the notable exception), because volume and cost can be large. Enable per service and log type (ADMIN_READ, DATA_READ, DATA_WRITE) in the IAM policy's `auditConfigs`, ideally at org level for sensitive services.
- **System Event**: Google-initiated changes such as live migration. Always on.
- **Policy Denied**: requests refused by VPC Service Controls or org policy.

Each entry's `protoPayload` holds `methodName`, `resourceName`, `authenticationInfo.principalEmail`, caller IP and the request.

Centralise them: an **aggregated sink** at the org or a folder with `--include-children` routes logs from every current and future project to one destination: a BigQuery dataset for analysis, a log bucket with **Log Analytics** and a locked retention policy, or Pub/Sub for a SIEM. Grant the sink's **writer identity** write access on the destination. Keep the destination in a dedicated security project that workload admins cannot touch.

Remember that audit logs show caller identities; with service account impersonation, `serviceAccountDelegationInfo` shows the original human.
concepts.code:
# Who changed IAM policies in prod this week?
gcloud logging read '
  logName:"cloudaudit.googleapis.com%2Factivity"
  AND protoPayload.methodName="SetIamPolicy"' \
  --project=shop-prod-1234 --freshness=7d \
  --format="table(timestamp,protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail,protoPayload.resourceName)"

# Route every audit log in the org to BigQuery in a security project
gcloud logging sinks create org-audit \
  bigquery.googleapis.com/projects/sec-logs-1234/datasets/org_audit \
  --organization=555555555555 --include-children --use-partitioned-tables \
  --log-filter='logName:"cloudaudit.googleapis.com"'

gcloud logging sinks describe org-audit --organization=555555555555 --format="value(writerIdentity)"
# serviceAccount:service-org-...@gcp-sa-logging.iam.gserviceaccount.com
# -> grant it roles/bigquery.dataEditor on the org_audit dataset
takeaways: Admin Activity is always on and free; Data Access is mostly off until enabled
Aggregated sinks with --include-children cover future projects too
Store audit logs in a separate, locked-down project
pitfalls: Assuming reads of sensitive data are logged when Data Access logs were never enabled for that service.

quiz.q: A secret was read last week and you need to know by whom, but nothing appears in logs. Most likely reason?
options: Data Access audit logs were not enabled for Secret Manager
quiz.explain: Reading a secret is a data access event, logged only when Data Access audit logs are enabled for the service.

concepts.name: GKE in production: identity and hardening
concepts.summary: Workload Identity Federation for GKE, private nodes and control-plane access, network policy, Binary Authorization and upgrade safety.
concepts.why: Default clusters run fine; secure, upgrade-safe clusters need deliberate identity, network and supply-chain controls.
concepts.body:
**Workload Identity Federation for GKE** gives each Kubernetes service account (KSA) its own IAM identity, so Pods call Google APIs without node service accounts or keys. You grant roles directly to a principal of the form `principal://iam.googleapis.com/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/PROJECT_ID.svc.id.goog/subject/ns/NAMESPACE/sa/KSA`. The GKE metadata server intercepts token requests from the Pod and exchanges them. It is enabled by default on Autopilot. Older setups instead bind a KSA to a Google service account via the `iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account` annotation.

Network hardening:

- **Private nodes** (no external IPs) with Cloud NAT for egress.
- Restrict the control plane endpoint: authorized networks, or the DNS-based endpoint protected by IAM.
- **Network policies** (enforced by GKE Dataplane V2) to default-deny traffic between namespaces.

Supply chain: **Binary Authorization** admits only images signed or attested by your pipeline, and Artifact Analysis scans for vulnerabilities. Keep node images on Container-Optimized OS with **Shielded GKE Nodes**.

Upgrade safety: GKE upgrades nodes by draining them, so give every workload replicas, a **PodDisruptionBudget**, readiness probes and graceful shutdown. Use maintenance windows and exclusions around critical periods, and watch deprecation insights before minor version upgrades.
concepts.code:
PROJECT=shop-dev-4821; NUM=987654321098
kubectl create namespace shop
kubectl create serviceaccount orders -n shop

# Grant the Kubernetes service account itself publish rights on one topic
gcloud pubsub topics add-iam-policy-binding orders --role=roles/pubsub.publisher \
  --member="principal://iam.googleapis.com/projects/$NUM/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/$PROJECT.svc.id.goog/subject/ns/shop/sa/orders"

# Pod spec: just run as that KSA; client libraries pick up the identity via ADC
kubectl -n shop patch deployment orders \
  -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"serviceAccountName":"orders"}}}}'

kubectl -n shop create poddisruptionbudget orders-pdb --selector=app=orders --min-available=1
takeaways: Grant IAM roles to Kubernetes service accounts via Workload Identity Federation
Private nodes, restricted control plane and network policies
PDBs, probes and replicas make automatic upgrades safe
pitfalls: Giving the node service account broad roles so every Pod on the node inherits them.

quiz.q: Why prefer Workload Identity Federation over granting roles to the node service account?
options: Permissions are scoped per Kubernetes service account instead of shared by all Pods on a node
It removes the need for IAM
quiz.explain: Node service account roles are available to every Pod on the node; WIF scopes them to one KSA.

concepts.name: Spanner internals: TrueTime and schema design
concepts.summary: How Spanner achieves external consistency with TrueTime, splits and Paxos, and how to design keys and interleaving to avoid hotspots.
concepts.why: Spanner performance depends almost entirely on primary key design, which only makes sense once you know how data is split.
concepts.body:
Spanner stores rows sorted by primary key and divides the key space into **splits**. Each split is replicated with **Paxos** across zones (or regions); one replica is the leader for writes. Spanner moves and splits ranges automatically based on load and size.

**TrueTime** is Google's clock API that returns an interval guaranteed to contain the real time, backed by GPS and atomic clocks. A read-write transaction picks a commit timestamp and performs a **commit wait** until that timestamp is certainly in the past. The result is **external consistency**: if T1 commits before T2 starts, T2's timestamp is larger, everywhere. Read-only transactions and stale reads can then be served lock-free from any up-to-date replica.

Design consequences:

- **Avoid monotonically increasing keys** (timestamps, auto-increment): all inserts land on the last split, a **hotspot**. Use UUIDv4, a hashed prefix, or a `bit_reversed_positive` sequence.
- **Interleave** child tables in their parent (`INTERLEAVE IN PARENT`) to store a parent's children physically next to it, making joins and transactions on one parent local.
- Keep transactions small; cross-split transactions use two-phase commit across Paxos groups.
- Use **stale reads** (e.g. 10 seconds) for read-heavy paths that tolerate slight lag.
takeaways: TrueTime + commit wait = external consistency
Sequential primary keys create write hotspots
Interleave children under parents for locality
pitfalls: Using a timestamp as the leading primary key column of a high-insert table.

quiz.q: Why is an auto-incrementing primary key a problem in Spanner?
options: All new rows land in the same split, creating a write hotspot
quiz.explain: Rows are range-split by key, so increasing keys always append to the last split.
